## Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

In this model of AI compute investment, the training-inference split, the timing of investment, and its scale respond to beliefs about the arrival of AGI in different ways. The training fraction has a closed form that rises with the arrival rate $\lambda$ and does not depend on scale (Proposition 1). Timing and scale are not monotone in beliefs: with the post-switch scale precommitted the single firm's trigger and capacity are hump-shaped in $\lambda$, and at baseline a single firm that chooses its scale when the switch arrives does not invest before it. Under competition one firm does, at every arrival rate examined, because waiting leads to a post-switch race in which the rent from leading is competed away (Proposition 3). At the date of first investment following is the better role, so competition brings investment forward of the switch without a race to be first, in an equilibrium that I verify numerically and do not show to be unique.

Three tensions drive the results. The first is current cash flow against future capability: firms balance inference revenue in regime $L$, which funds operations and services debt, against training whose payoff arrives only in regime $H$. The optimal training fraction $\phi^*$ increases in $\lambda$, so a firm that expects the switch sooner trains more. The second is the continuation value against the risk of stopping. Operating costs create a boundary at which the firm stops operating whether or not it has debt, and leverage shifts it. The *faith-based survival* channel holds at the calibrated optimum but not throughout the parameter space: its $A_{\text{eff}}$-channel threshold $\underline{\phi} \approx 0.18$ lies well below $\phi^* \approx 0.70$, so at baseline a firm that trains more because it expects the switch sooner sits further from default (Proposition 2). At a fixed belief, by contrast, the boundary is U-shaped in the training fraction with its minimum at $\phi^*$, so training beyond the optimum raises it, and the channel reverses for beliefs below $\lambda \approx 0.034$. Creditors gain little on either side of the split: recovery is at most $5\%$ of the claim at the model's policies, so credit risk there is the risk of reaching the boundary (@sec-valuation).

The third is the cost of belief mismatches (@sec-valuation). In Numerical Finding 1, for a single firm with precommitted post-switch scale and values measured at half the informed firm's trigger, a pessimistic error costs more in expected value than an optimistic error of the same size in $\lambda$, $32\%$ against $1.3\%$ around a true rate of $0.10$, mainly because under-allocating to training gives up the post-switch claim that makes up most of an installed firm's value. The ranking depends on how the errors are matched: at a factor of five in either direction the losses are $32\%$ and $13\%$, and for equal errors in the expected time to the switch they are about equal, the optimist's being slightly larger. Tail exposure runs the other way for proportional errors. The far optimist enters at a lower trigger with an allocation that depresses pre-switch revenue, which leaves it closer to the boundary at which it stops operating: its five-year probability of reaching that boundary is $1.8\%$ without debt against $0.16\%$ at correct beliefs, and $4.3\%$ against $0.47\%$ at $\ell = 0.40$ under fairly priced debt (no-switch upper bounds on the pre-switch probability). The belief sets most of this exposure, and leverage adds to it. This is not a general case for building more. Moderate optimism is cheap, $1.3\%$ of value at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.18$, and extreme optimism is not, $13\%$ at $\lambda_{\text{invest}} = 0.50$ (@fig-investment-dilemma); with scale chosen at the switch, every belief from $0.073$ up prescribes waiting and costs nothing. Aggressive commitments are therefore compatible with a moderately optimistic belief at small cost, though the model separates neither beliefs from signaling nor either from agency motives, and the calibration is stylized.

The model abstracts from talent constraints, alignment objectives, geopolitical competition, entrants such as DeepSeek [@deepseek2025r1], and a \$600 billion gap between AI infrastructure spending and current AI revenue [@cahn2024gap] that may discipline the race through financial markets before any of these other forces do. Three extensions follow directly: dynamic learning about $\lambda$, dynamic reallocation, and financial frictions. The central point is simpler than any of them. The split between training and inference is the decision through which a belief about the switch becomes a position: it sets what the firm is worth if the switch comes and how far demand can fall before the firm stops operating. In this model a firm that is too cautious about the timeline pays mostly in expected value, and one that is far too bold pays less in value and more in the risk of stopping.
